definition: Eloquent means using language so fluently and movingly that it stirs the audience.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word eloquent. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know eloquent should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Nobody expected the quiet groundskeeper to deliver the evening's most eloquent speech, but by the end even the caterers had stopped to listen.
Fluent is milder than eloquent: fluent speech flows without a stumble, but flow alone moves no one — eloquent speech has the ease and the power to stir its audience.
Spellbinding goes beyond eloquent: an eloquent speaker moves the room, while a spellbinding one suspends it — nobody shifts, coughs, or checks the time until the voice stops.
Articulate praises clarity: thoughts put into words cleanly and in good order. Eloquent starts there and adds power — eloquent language does not just inform its audience, it moves them.

Silver-tongued admires persuasive charm, often with a raised eyebrow — the word hints the speaker could sell anything. Eloquent is admiration without the suspicion: moving language offered in earnest.

Actors say the sword fights are the easy part; it's the soliloquies they rehearse at two in the morning.
Eloquent means using language so fluently and movingly that it stirs the audience.

Asked to say a few words at the bridge dedication, the retired ferry captain proved unexpectedly eloquent: he spoke of thirty years reading the river's moods, of couples who met aboard and married ashore, and when he finished, the applause waited a beat — people were wiping their eyes first.
Eloquent is the exact word because the speech did more than come out clearly: it moved people, and the pause before the applause is the measure.
Articulate would credit the clarity alone; eloquent credits language with power — fluency in the service of feeling.
Eloquent is praise, and it can land on more than speeches: an eloquent letter, an eloquent silence, an eloquent shrug — anything that expresses powerfully.
Keep it apart from elegant, which praises how something looks, not how it speaks; the SAT likes that near-miss.
Beside its neighbors: articulate is clear, fluent is smooth, and eloquent is the one that moves people.

The new bridge had three senators, a brass band, and a ribbon the width of a truck.
But the dedication is remembered for Amos Reyes, ninety-one, one of the original welders, who was handed the microphone almost as an afterthought.
He spoke for four minutes without notes about the men who had built the old span — the winters, the wet rope, the two who never came home.
He repeated himself once and lost his place once.
And still, when he finished, the senators stood with everyone else, and nobody reached for a camera.
Reporters who had heard a thousand speeches called it the most eloquent four minutes of the year.
